passages.title: Email Correspondence: A Donated Collection and Its Label

emails.subject: The Okafor textile collection — display caption
emails.body:
Dear Dr Ashcombe,

My grandmother donated forty-one textiles to the museum in 1994. I visited the new gallery last week and I want to raise the caption rather than the display, which is beautifully done.

The caption reads "Donated by an anonymous benefactor, 1994". My grandmother was not anonymous. She signed the deed of gift, she attended the opening, and there is a photograph of her doing so in your own archive. She asked for no publicity at the time, which I understand may be where this originates, but asking for no publicity in 1994 is not the same as wishing to be unnamed in perpetuity, and she died in 2011 without ever being asked the second question.

I am not asserting a legal right. I have read the deed and it says nothing about attribution either way, so I accept this is a decision the museum is entitled to make.

What I am asking is that it be made rather than inherited. If someone weighs it and concludes she should remain unnamed, I will accept that and I would like to know the reasoning. What I would find hard is learning that the caption says anonymous because a card written in 1994 said anonymous and nobody has looked at it since.

With respect,
Amaka Nwosu-Bright

emails.subject: RE: The Okafor textile collection — display caption
emails.body:
Dear Ms Nwosu-Bright,

It was inherited, exactly as you describe. The 1994 accession card records "donor requests no publicity" and every subsequent caption has rendered that as "anonymous benefactor". Nobody weighed it, because nobody noticed there was anything to weigh.

I have now looked at the file. Your grandmother's letter of 12 March 1994 says she does not wish the gift "announced in the press". It says nothing about the label. Those are different requests and we collapsed them.

The caption will be changed to name her. I am not going to present that as generosity — it is a correction, and it should read as one.

The deed does give the museum discretion over attribution, and you are right about that, but discretion exercised once in 1994 by inference and never revisited is not really discretion. I would rather say that plainly than rely on it.

Three further things.

We hold the photograph you mention. It will go into the gallery with the collection, with her name, if you and your family are content — I would like your agreement before I display an image of her rather than after.

I have asked for an audit of accession records where "no publicity" has been rendered as "anonymous". There are, on a first look, at least nineteen. I do not know yet how many are the same error.

And I cannot restore the twenty-nine years. The correction runs forward. I am aware that is the part that matters least to a museum and most to a family.

With thanks,
Helena Ashcombe

passages.title: How Museums Decide What to Keep
passages.content:
Museums are popularly imagined as places that keep things, and the assumption behind that image — that a collection grows and is preserved indefinitely — describes almost no institution accurately. Most of what a museum holds is never displayed, and the decisions that shape a collection are made about storage, cost and disposal at least as often as about acquisition.

The proportions surprise people. A typical museum displays a small fraction of what it holds; the rest sits in stores that must be climate-controlled, insured, catalogued and periodically conserved. Every object accepted therefore carries a permanent liability, and an institution accepting a donation is committing successors to a cost with no end date. This is why refusal is more common than the public expects, and why it is rarely explained: declining a gift offered in good faith is awkward, and museums generally decline quietly.

Disposal — deaccessioning — is more common than the sector's reticence suggests and is governed by strict conditions in most professional codes, typically requiring that proceeds be used for collections rather than for running costs. That restriction exists because the alternative creates an obvious incentive: an institution in financial difficulty holding valuable objects would otherwise be tempted to solve one problem by liquidating another. The rule is unpopular during funding crises and is defended precisely because that is when it matters.

What gets kept is also shaped by what was collectable at the time. Nineteenth and early twentieth-century collecting concentrated on the durable, the exotic and the elite, so museums hold a great deal about a few people and very little about most. Ordinary domestic objects, working clothes and the material culture of the poor survive at far lower rates, not because they were valued less by their owners but because nobody was acquiring them. A collection is a record of past collecting priorities before it is a record of the past.

Documentation is the quiet determinant of value. An object with a known origin, owner and date supports research; the same object without that information is decorative. Museums frequently hold both, and the difference between them is not the object but a card written or not written when it arrived — which is why cataloguing backlogs, unglamorous and chronically underfunded, do more damage than most acquisitions do good.

viewpoints.name: Director Ottoline Bergqvist
viewpoints.text: We removed admission charges and visits rose sharply, which is the figure everyone quotes back at me. The figure I would rather discuss is that the demographic profile of our visitors barely changed. Free entry removed a barrier for people who were already inclined to come and were choosing between us and a coffee; it did not reach people for whom the barrier was never the ticket. I would keep free entry, and I would stop describing it as an access measure when what it actually is is a volume measure.

viewpoints.name: Rafael Quintero, museum finance officer
viewpoints.text: The debate is conducted as though the alternative to charging is free, when in practice the alternative is a different charge. We are free at the door and we charge for exhibitions, workshops, the family trail and the audio guide, because the funding has to come from somewhere. A family visiting us on a Saturday can easily spend more than a single admission fee would have cost them, in smaller amounts they did not plan for. I am not arguing for admission charges. I am arguing that we stop calling this free without a footnote.

viewpoints.name: Dr Marguerite Osei, cultural economist
viewpoints.text: The evidence that free entry increases visits is robust. The evidence that it broadens the audience is weak and consistently weaker than the sector's advocacy suggests, because the binding constraints for non-visitors are travel cost, time, childcare and a belief that the institution is not for them — none of which a ticket price addresses. I support free entry on other grounds. What I object to is a policy justified by an effect it has repeatedly been shown not to have.

viewpoints.name: Idris Nakamura, secondary school teacher
viewpoints.text: Free entry changed what I can do. I bring four classes a year now and I brought one before, because the coach is the cost I cannot avoid and admission was the one I could remove. That is a real effect and it is invisible in visitor demographics, because my students are counted as general visitors and nobody records that they came as a group who otherwise would not have. I would only add that free entry with a compulsory booking system and a two-term waiting list is not free entry for a school.
